editorial.headline: Used Household Retail: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Used household furnishings sit within a nationally open activity, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium closes the registration route for this trade.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register a PMA business for this activity in Bali today. That outcome is not a judgement on the trade itself; it follows Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The contrast is decisive: national openness does not create a Bali registration path where the provincial rule blocks it.

The activity is retail trade in used household equipment. Its subject is recognisably domestic: used tables, chairs, wardrobes, beds and sideboards, together with used items for eating and drinking. The category is shaped by the character of the goods being offered at retail—their previous use and their household purpose. It gives a clear commercial home to a retail operation built around second-hand furnishings and household dining items, whether the stock centres on larger pieces of furniture or the practical objects that accompany life at home.

Registration is open across the full set of enterprise scales recorded here: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the activity is not presented as belonging only to a small trader or only to a larger operator. The record permits the same retail subject at each of those scales. For a founder, the useful discipline is to keep the activity description equally clear: the business is retailing used household equipment, not merely dealing in goods that happen to have been used.

Bali changes the practical conclusion for PMA registration. The OSS risk assessment at the Large scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, placing the activity within the class caught by the Bali moratorium dated May 2026. Bali’s status is therefore blocked on risk-class grounds, notwithstanding the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. A founder considering this activity should read those two facts together: it is fully open to foreign ownership at the national level, but a foreigner cannot register it as PMA in Bali under the stated provincial rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not create a Bali registration path where the provincial rule blocks it.
